current_truth: A robust source contract should store each guide or static-data statement as one atomic, typed claim with exact deck or card scope, short evidence text, per-claim provenance, and a separate readiness or confidence state. Fixed `claim_kind` vocabularies, explicit negative assertions, and non-blocking static fallback are the safest structure for HSConfig because absence of guide evidence is not the same as a negative fact, while deterministic card registries and deckstrings can still provide identity and bounded semantic support for any deck.
source_backed_claims: W3C PROV-DM and PROV-O define an extensible but interoperable provenance model built around entities, activities, agents, and bundles, which fits per-claim source metadata and provenance-of-provenance rather than deck-level free text. Sources: https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/ and https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/

JSON Schema recommends fixed enumerations for closed value sets, so `claim_kind`, `source_confidence`, `claim_readiness`, and `trust_ceiling` should stay closed vocabularies instead of free text. Source: https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/reference/enum

JSON Schema also supports conditional requirements, which maps cleanly to source-contract rules such as requiring `cards` for card claims, `sequence` for combo claims, or runtime hints only for claim kinds that can legally lower. Source: https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/reference/conditionals

OWL 2 distinguishes the open-world assumption from database-style closed-world reasoning: missing facts may simply be missing, not false. The same primer also highlights explicit negative property assertions for facts known to be untrue. That supports a contract rule that omission must not become `mulligan_discard`, `known_bad_pattern`, or any other negative claim without explicit evidence. Sources: https://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-primer/ and https://www.w3.org/2007/OWL/draft/ED-owl2-primer-20090531/

PaperTrail shows a concrete claim-evidence design in which source documents and answers are decomposed into discrete claims and evidence links, revealing supported claims, unsupported claims, and omissions. That is strong evidence for storing claim coverage and negative evidence explicitly instead of compressing whole guides into one row. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21045

The W3C uncertainty report argues that machine-readable information often remains incomplete or partially correct and should preserve differences in confidence and trust rather than flatten them to Boolean truth. That supports explicit low or report-only labels in HSConfig. Source: https://www.w3.org/2005/Incubator/urw3/group/draftReport.html

HearthSim deckstrings losslessly encode a deck and use DBF IDs, while HearthstoneJSON `cards.json` includes every card, including heroes, hero powers, and buffs. That makes them suitable non-blocking fallback sources for identity resolution and static semantics, but not for strategic guide intent. Sources: https://hearthsim.info/docs/deckstrings/ and https://hearthstonejson.com/docs/cards.html

The current HSConfig repo already aligns with this pattern: `source_document_model.py` constrains supported atomic claim kinds and blocks runtime lowering for `explicit_low_confidence`, `generic_low_confidence`, and `contract_gap`; `source_document_builder.py` assigns `source_backed_static_semantics` to static card sources; `semantic_enrichment.py` marks fallback enrichment as `non_blocking`; and `research_contract.py` suppresses negative keep behavior from generic text alone. risk_to_hsconfig: Free-text heuristics can over-infer strategy. If HSConfig treats the word `keep` or positive phrasing as enough for `mulligan_keep`, start-of-game enablers can be misclassified as opening-hand keeps.
Guide omission can be misread as negative evidence. Under an open-world reading, a guide not naming a card is usually incomplete evidence, not proof that the card should be discarded or never played.

Static card metadata can be over-read into gameplay intent. Card text, hero power links, keywords, and registry fields support identity and mechanics, but they do not justify matchup-specific keeps, exact combo timing, or target priority by themselves.
Confidence inflation is easy if multiple weak paraphrases are merged into one stronger row or if stale source material is kept at `high` without freshness downgrades.
Fallback enrichment can become unsafe if built-in supplements silently produce runtime-lowerable claims instead of bounded `static_semantics` or report-only support.

Deck-level prose can drift into unsupported lowerings when claim scope is vague, for example when an archetype-level statement is converted into a card-specific runtime behavior without explicit evidence.
recommended_contract_rule: Keep `claim_kind` as a strict enum and reject or quarantine unsupported values instead of coercing them into nearby meanings.
Store one atomic proposition per claim row: one claim id, one `claim_kind`, one scope, one confidence state, one short evidence string, and one provenance packet.

Separate strategic guide claims from deterministic static-semantic claims. `mulligan_keep`, `mulligan_discard`, `targeting_rule`, `combo_sequence`, and `gameplan_posture` should require explicit guide evidence, while identity and mechanic facts from registry text should stay in `source_backed_static_semantics` or an equivalent bounded lane.

Represent negative evidence explicitly. Use negative claim kinds, negative stance, or contradiction markers for facts such as `do not keep`, `avoid this line`, or `known bad pattern`; do not derive them from absence alone.

Preserve claim coverage state. Track whether each candidate claim is supported, unsupported, omitted, contradicted, or fallback-only so that research debt stays visible instead of being silently compressed.
Use two confidence layers: `source_confidence` for what the source itself supports, and `claim_readiness` or `trust_ceiling` for what the contract is allowed to lower into runtime.

Allow non-blocking fallback for any deck only on deterministic surfaces such as deck decode, card identity, collectible status, hero power links, and stable text-derived mechanics. Mark the result as bounded semantic support, not guide-backed strategy.
When sources are weak or unresolved, emit warnings, gap rows, or report-only claims rather than failing the whole deck or inventing confident runtime output.
Keep freshness in the contract. If a source is stale, automatically downgrade confidence rather than preserving an inherited `high` label.
never_infer: Never infer `mulligan_keep` or `mulligan_discard` from generic praise, generic criticism, or the word `keep` appearing in unrelated effect descriptions.
Never infer matchup advice, turn-order advice, or exact combo timing from deckstrings or static card text alone.
Never infer a target selector, discover choice, choose-one choice, or exact combo sequence unless the source or deterministic game rule explicitly names the relation.
Never infer that a card is strategically irrelevant because a guide omits it.
Never infer runtime-lowerable confidence from source count alone when the sources are stale, vague, duplicated, or paraphrased from each other.
Never infer generated-entity or hero-power identity from loose name similarity when registry lookup and supplement resolution do not confirm the link.
confidence_model: Confidence should flow in layers. First, score the source statement itself using source type, specificity, freshness, and whether the evidence text names exact deck cards or only generic archetype ideas. Second, derive `claim_readiness` from both confidence and claim family: explicit card-specific guide claims may become `guide_backed`; deterministic registry or card-text semantics may become `source_backed_static_semantics`; archetype-only summaries become `archetype_inferred`; weak, stale, or generic statements stay `explicit_low_confidence`, `generic_low_confidence`, or `contract_gap`. Third, runtime lowering should depend on readiness and trust ceiling, not just on optimistic wording. Positive and negative claims for the same card or scope should be reconciled explicitly, while omission alone should not demote a claim into a negative. Final deck confidence should aggregate supported claim coverage, unresolved gaps, and fallback usage rather than inheriting the strongest single row.
validation_implications: Add or keep schema tests that only accepted `claim_kind` enum values are normalized, and that unsupported values land in an unsupported-claims report instead of silently lowering.
Require core provenance keys per claim: source URL, source title, source family, retrieved date, short evidence text, and source confidence.
Add conditional validation tests so card claims require exact deck card ids, combo claims require exact sequences, and deck-scoped claims cannot masquerade as card-specific claims.
Add regression tests proving omission does not create a negative claim. Only explicit negative evidence should create `mulligan_discard`, `known_bad_pattern`, or other negative rows.

Add paired positive and negative fixture cases for effect enablers, including the existing ShadowPriest split where the start-of-game transform remains encoded but the card is not emitted as a mulligan keep.
Keep runtime-lowering tests that low-confidence, report-only, fallback-only, and contract-gap claims cannot alter Mulligan, per-card CardID behavior, Combo, or GlobalValues surfaces.

Add deck-agnostic fallback tests showing that any valid deckstring can still produce identity and static-semantic reports from HearthstoneJSON plus supplements without inventing strategic guide claims.
Extend coverage accounting tests so research output can report supported, unsupported, omitted, contradicted, and fallback-only claim counts, not just broad pass-fail status.
